components.text: The cited testimony must be early enough and specific enough to identify the surviving canonical four rather than later naming tradition.
Geographic agreement must provide independent corroboration rather than merely repeated later attribution.
Whether the cited testimony securely and unambiguously attributes the surviving canonical four before the late second century.
Whether geographic spread and agreement demonstrate independent preservation rather than later diffusion.
The inference from an eyewitness beloved disciple to John as the final literary author or controlling authority must be established.
The proposed assistance and Semitic-material scenario must bridge the education required for sophisticated Greek composition.
Whether identifying an eyewitness source as John establishes that John possessed or controlled the literary capacity producing the final Greek Gospel.
Whether a proposed Semitic precursor and supervised Greek version adequately bridge Matthew's educational and compositional limitations.
The consistent later names require an explanation that distinguishes preserved authorial knowledge from a common attribution process.
The relative prominence of the four selected names must fit the proposed authority-conferring motive.
Whether early and geographically diverse attribution is better explained by preserved authorial knowledge than by a later common naming origin.
A chronological gap between composition and explicit attribution must show that traditional authorship is historically unreliable.
Papias and Justin must fail to provide earlier support specific enough to reduce the asserted attribution gap.
The later authority-conferring naming explanation must outperform continuity from earlier testimony.
Whether anonymous composition and a long delay before unambiguous attribution make traditional authorship historically inadequate.
Whether Papias and Justin unambiguously identify the surviving canonical texts rather than related traditions or other writings.
Justin's reference to Peter's memoirs must specifically support canonical Mark rather than another Petrine Gospel tradition.
Justin's terminology and textual agreements must independently corroborate Mark's derivation from Peter.
Whether Justin's memoirs of Peter provide early evidence linking canonical Mark with Peter.
Whether internal Petrine features independently support Peter as the source behind canonical Mark.
A prestige-driven naming hypothesis must explain selection of Mark and Luke rather than more prominent direct disciples.
The selected names must be compared with the more marketable names used in later apocryphal Gospels.
Whether an authority-conferring fabrication would plausibly select the comparatively minor non-eyewitness names Mark and Luke.
Whether Matthew and John, together with Mark and Luke, form a coherent strategically authoritative fourfold set.
The naming hypothesis must explain why comparatively minor Mark and Luke could still confer substantial apostolic authority.
The four-name pattern must provide a coherent representation of principal apostolic witness.
Whether Mark and Luke were too minor to serve the authority-conferring purposes of a fabricated attribution scheme.
Whether later apocryphal preference for direct disciples makes companion attributions historically unlikely.
Matthew's tax and money vocabulary must discriminate a tax-collector author from other possible authors.
The fiscal feature must do more than remain merely consistent with traditional Matthean authorship.
Whether Matthew's greater attention to taxes and money is probative evidence that its author was a tax collector.
Whether early tradition and the proposed Semitic-to-Greek production history independently support Matthew's involvement.
Identifying the beloved disciple as a witness must also identify that witness as the final writer of the Gospel.
Multiple later attributions must be shown independent rather than repetitions after a naming tradition begins.
The Gospel's closing collective voice must be reconciled with direct authorship by the beloved disciple.
Whether identifying the beloved disciple as an eyewitness source also identifies him as the final Gospel's literary author.
Whether geographically dispersed later witnesses are independent evidence once a common naming tradition has begun.
Geographically widespread later agreement must demonstrate independent memory rather than diffusion from one common naming origin.
Justin's failure to name Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John must be reconciled with a claimed continuous early attribution tradition.
Whether later universal agreement and geographic spread independently establish that the traditional names accompanied the Gospels from composition.
Whether Justin's failure to use the four traditional names is compatible with an already established early attribution tradition.
Ancient assistance evidence must support delegation of sophisticated long-form Greek Gospel composition, not merely routine letter writing.
The proposed assistant must preserve a defensible sense in which Matthew remained author or controlling authority.
Whether ancient assistance practices can bridge from limited personal literary capacity to production of a long sophisticated Greek Gospel.
Whether analogies with other ancient attribution practices establish comparable delegation of full narrative composition.
Traditional responsibility must explain sophisticated Greek composition without relying only on short-letter secretarial analogies.
The production account must bridge the asserted educational mismatch for Matthew's Greek composition.
Use of an underlying source must still identify the final author or controlling authority with a traditional figure.
Whether the proposed production model requires an amanuensis to originate a long sophisticated narrative rather than assist with source-based composition.
Whether Matthew's limited educational background is compatible with Greek composition through assistance and extensive written sources.
Whether financial vocabulary independently identifies Matthew as the author.
